Share of Search as a complement to brand tracking

A pilot study on 50 Australian categories — Tracksuit DS take-home

Zen

16 August 2026

Summary for non-technical readers

What we did. We collected 3.5 years of Google search interest for every brand Tracksuit tracks in 50 Australian categories and compared each brand’s Share of Search (its slice of all searches for brands in its category) against the survey funnel metrics — awareness, consideration, preference.

What we found.

Search ranks brands the way the survey does — but only in some categories. In about a third of the categories we tested, Share of Search reproduces the survey’s competitive ranking closely; in another third it is essentially uninformative. Which is which is predictable in advance, and that predictability is what makes this usable: we set out measurable criteria for whether a category qualifies. About one brand in five has no measurable search demand at all.

Search cannot yet replace the survey for tracking movement. Month-to-month changes in consideration are mostly survey sampling noise at n≈200 — and we show that this, not search quality, is what caps any correlation. Search may in fact be the steadier signal in low-sample categories.

Search shows a hint of leading consideration by two to three months (suggestive under a placebo test, not yet established) — consistent with published evidence that Share of Search leads market share by 6–12 months. If it holds up under further validation, this is the most commercially interesting property: an early-warning indicator between survey waves.

What we recommend. Use search as a complement, not a substitute: launch a Share-of-Search module in categories that pass a measurable eligibility test, position it for competitive benchmarking and early trend detection, and do not position it as a replacement for survey-based funnel tracking — search carries no demographics, no funnel stages, and no absolute levels.

(Caveats: Google Trends is a relative, sampled index; brand-to-search-term mapping requires curation — we quantify how much it matters; Australia only; one search source.)

1. The question

Share of Search (SoS) is increasingly cited as a cheap proxy for brand strength. But “does search correlate with our metrics?” is really two different product questions:

  1. Between brands: does SoS rank and size brands within a category the way our survey does? If yes, search could substitute for parts of competitive benchmarking.
  2. Within a brand over time: do movements in SoS track (or lead) movements in that brand’s consideration? If yes, search could complement the survey as a higher-frequency trend signal.

These have different bars to clear and different failure modes, so we test them separately, on the same data.

Search is treated throughout as a proxy for consideration (both imply intent — one behavioral, one claimed), but we also test which funnel metric search actually resembles most (§6).

2. Data

2.1 Survey data

survey |>
  summarise(categories = n_distinct(category_name),
            `brand-category pairs` = n_distinct(paste(category_name, brand_name)),
            waves = n_distinct(wave_date),
            first_wave = min(wave_date), last_wave = max(wave_date))

Monthly syndicated tracking, ~200 qualified respondents per category-wave. Funnel metrics: prompted awareness, consideration, preference.

2.2 Search data

Google Trends, Australia, monthly, September 2021 – March 2025, collected by pull/pull_trends.py (see pull/README.md):

  • Brands are resolved to Google knowledge-graph topic entities where a credible one exists (the main defense against homonyms — Koala the mattress vs the animal, Mecca the retailer vs the city), with hand-curated terms for the pilot categories and every resolution logged for review.
  • Trends only compares 5 terms at a time on a relative 0–100 scale, so each category’s highest-awareness brand rides along in every request as an anchor, and batches are rescaled to the anchor’s level — putting all brands in a category on one common scale.
  • Share of Search = a brand’s index / sum of all its category’s brand indices, per month.
trends |>
  summarise(categories = n_distinct(category_name),
            `brand-category pairs` = n_distinct(paste(category_name, brand_name)),
            months = n_distinct(month))
vol <- trends |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(mean_idx = mean(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
searchable_share <- mean(vol$mean_idx >= VOL_MIN)

A finding before any correlation: only 81% of tracked brands register measurable search volume at all. Two failure modes are deliberately separated here. Resolution failure — a brand whose search entity can’t be identified — is a fixable data problem, and the pipeline handles it automatically (a topic entity that returns an empty series is re-pulled as the raw brand name before we conclude anything). What remains is genuine absence of search demand: the long tail of survey-tracked brands that Australians simply do not search for at measurable volume. That is a property of the market, not the pipeline — it alone rules out search as a full survey substitute, and it becomes the first criterion of the eligibility framework (§8). Brands below the volume floor are excluded from SoS computations below.

3. How much signal is even in the survey?

Before correlating anything we ask what a correlation against monthly survey metrics could possibly achieve. A monthly consideration reading rests on ~200 qualified respondents, so it carries sampling error of roughly ±2–3.5pp. Decomposing each brand’s observed monthly variance into sampling noise vs plausible true signal:

nd <- noise_decomposition(survey, "consideration")
nd_cat <- nd |> filter(waves >= 12) |>
  group_by(category_name) |>
  summarise(brands = n(), mean_reliability = mean(reliability, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_max_r = mean(max_attainable_r, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

median_se <- survey |> mutate(se = se_prop(consideration, base_n)) |>
  summarise(m = median(se, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(m)

ggplot(nd_cat, aes(mean_reliability, reorder(category_name, mean_reliability))) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL[1], width = .75) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  labs(x = "Share of monthly variance in consideration that is true signal",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Most monthly movement in consideration is sampling noise",
       subtitle = paste0("Reliability = 1 − sampling var / observed var, averaged over brands. ",
                         "Median monthly SE ±", round(median_se * 100, 1), "pp."))

For 74% of brands, less than half of monthly variance is signal. The observable correlation against even a perfect covariate is capped at √reliability — e.g. ~0.3 for Car Insurance at monthly grain. Two design consequences:

  • All within-brand analysis uses quarterly (3-month rolling) smoothing.
  • Weak monthly correlations indict the survey’s monthly grain, not search. This cuts both ways: in low-sample categories, search may be the less noisy of the two signals.

4. Between brands: does SoS rank brands like the survey does?

For each category we compare brands’ average SoS against their average share of consideration (consideration renormalized across the same searchable brand set, so both shares live on one denominator).

sos <- trends |>
  semi_join(vol |> filter(mean_idx >= VOL_MIN),
            by = c("category_name", "brand_name")) |>
  group_by(category_name, month) |>
  mutate(sos = trends_index / sum(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

joined <- survey |>
  inner_join(sos |> select(category_name, brand_name, month, trends_index, sos),
             by = c("category_name", "brand_name", "wave_date" = "month")) |>
  group_by(category_name, wave_date) |>
  mutate(soc = consideration / sum(consideration, na.rm = TRUE),
         soa = awareness / sum(awareness, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(conversion = if_else(awareness > 0, consideration / awareness, NA_real_))

between_brand <- joined |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(across(c(sos, soc, soa, consideration, awareness, conversion),
                   ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop")

between_cat <- between_brand |>
  group_by(category_name) |>
  filter(n() >= 4) |>
  summarise(n_brands = n(),
            rho_soc = cor(sos, soc, method = "spearman"),
            rho_aware = cor(sos, soa, method = "spearman"),
            rho_conv = cor(sos, conversion, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
            .groups = "drop")
ggplot(between_cat,
       aes(rho_soc, reorder(category_name, rho_soc),
           color = category_name %in% PILOTS)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey55", `TRUE` = PAL[2]),
                     labels = c(`FALSE` = "Other", `TRUE` = "Pilot (curated terms)"),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman rank correlation: mean SoS vs mean share of consideration",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Share of Search reproduces the survey's brand ranking in most categories",
       subtitle = paste0("Median ρ = ",
                         round(median(between_cat$rho_soc, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
                         "; categories with ≥4 searchable brands"))

pb <- between_brand |> filter(category_name %in% PILOTS)
lab <- pb |> group_by(category_name) |>
  mutate(resid = abs(rank(sos) - rank(soc))) |>
  slice_max(resid, n = 2)
ggplot(pb, aes(soc, sos)) +
  geom_abline(color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = PAL[1], size = 2) +
  ggrepel_or_text(lab) +
  facet_wrap(~category_name, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "Share of consideration (survey)", y = "Share of Search",
       title = "Pilot categories: brand-level agreement and interpretable outliers",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect share agreement. Labeled points are the largest rank disagreements.")

Interpretation:

  • Agreement is category-specific, not general. The median category sits near ρ = 0.4, but the distribution is wide: roughly a third of categories clear ρ ≥ 0.7 (Department Stores, Fast Food, Car Insurance, Online Marketplaces — large brands, distinct names, real search demand), while a tail sits at or below zero (Haircare, Men’s Online Health Providers, Healthy Beverages — thin, niche, own-brand-heavy fields where most brands barely register). This spread is the finding: it is what makes an eligibility framework (§8) necessary rather than a blanket rollout.
  • The disagreements are diagnosable, not random. Suncorp and RACQ over-index in search because people search them for banking and roadside assistance, not car insurance (intent mix); The Bottle-O over-indexes because “bottle-o” is Australian slang for any liquor store. A brand’s residual from this line is itself interpretable, which is a feature: it flags where search intent and brand intent diverge.
  • A methodological note worth stating plainly. An earlier iteration of this analysis reported a higher median ρ (0.62) — because a data-quality bug had silently zeroed out ~90 brands, which the volume floor then excluded. Fixing the bug added those brands back, and they are precisely the small, hard-to-rank ones. Cleaner data produced a weaker headline number. That is the correct direction of travel: the earlier figure was a selection artifact, and anyone benchmarking SoS should ask what was dropped before believing a high correlation.

5. Within brands: does SoS track movement over time?

Quarterly-smoothed SoS vs share of consideration, within each brand.

q <- joined |>
  smooth_quarterly(c("sos", "soc")) |>
  filter(!is.na(sos_q), !is.na(soc_q))

within_brand <- q |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  filter(n() >= 10, sd(sos_q) > 0, sd(soc_q) > 0) |>
  summarise(r_within = cor(sos_q, soc_q), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(nd |> select(category_name, brand_name, max_attainable_r),
            by = c("category_name", "brand_name"))
ggplot(within_brand, aes(r_within)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .1, fill = PAL[1], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(r_within)), color = PAL[2], linewidth = .8) +
  annotate("text", x = median(within_brand$r_within) + .03, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("median = ", round(median(within_brand$r_within), 2)),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, color = PAL[2]) +
  labs(x = "Within-brand correlation (quarterly SoS vs share of consideration)",
       y = "Brands",
       title = "Within-brand tracking is weak on average — but the ceiling is low too",
       subtitle = paste0("Mean attainable ceiling from survey noise ≈ ",
                         round(mean(within_brand$max_attainable_r, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
                         " even for a perfect covariate"))

The distribution centers near zero with wide spread. Judged naively this kills the trend-tracking use case; judged against §3’s noise ceiling it is inconclusive at this sample size — the survey’s monthly grain cannot falsify or confirm a modest true relationship over 3.5 years. What the data can say:

  • A minority of brands (large, dynamic ones — e.g. Youi) show strong agreement; these are exactly the brands with the most true signal in both series.
  • Regressions on within-brand standardized series (each brand’s SoS and share-of-consideration centered and scaled before pooling — the demeaning step of a brand fixed-effects estimator) give small positive coefficients in most categories — directionally right, small, and attenuated by noise in both variables.

5.1 Does search lead consideration?

leadlag <- purrr::map_dfr(-3:3, function(k) {
  q |>
    group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
    arrange(wave_date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(sos_l = if (k >= 0) lag(sos_q, k) else lead(sos_q, -k)) |>
    filter(!is.na(sos_l), !is.na(soc_q)) |>
    group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
    filter(n() >= 10, sd(sos_l) > 0, sd(soc_q) > 0) |>
    summarise(r = cor(sos_l, soc_q), .groups = "drop") |>
    summarise(lag_months = k, mean_r = mean(r), n_brands = n())
})

ggplot(leadlag, aes(lag_months, mean_r)) +
  geom_col(fill = ifelse(leadlag$lag_months > 0, PAL[1], "grey70"), width = .7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3,
                     labels = c("-3", "-2", "-1", "0", "+1", "+2", "+3")) +
  labs(x = "SoS shifted by k months (positive = search earlier than survey)",
       y = "Mean within-brand correlation",
       title = "Search interest weakly leads surveyed consideration",
       subtitle = "Correlation is highest when SoS is shifted 2–3 months ahead of the survey")

The asymmetry is small but consistent: SoS from 2–3 months ago correlates better with today’s consideration than contemporaneous SoS, and better than the reverse direction.

Placebo check. To test whether any of this is brand-level signal rather than category seasonality, we reassign each SoS series to a random other brand in the same category (100 permutations) and recompute the whole curve (analysis/03_leadlag_placebo.R):

plc <- readr::read_csv("out/leadlag_placebo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
band <- plc |> filter(run != "real") |> group_by(lag_months) |>
  summarise(lo = quantile(mean_r, .025), hi = quantile(mean_r, .975))
real_c <- plc |> filter(run == "real")
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(lag_months, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
              fill = "grey85") +
  annotate("text", x = -3, y = max(band$hi), hjust = 0, vjust = -0.4,
           label = "placebo range", color = "grey45", size = 3.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = real_c, aes(lag_months, mean_r), color = PAL[1], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = real_c, aes(lag_months, mean_r), color = PAL[1], size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3) +
  labs(x = "SoS shifted by k months (positive = search earlier than survey)",
       y = "Mean within-brand correlation",
       title = "The brand-level link is real; the lead asymmetry is suggestive",
       subtitle = "Grey band = 95% range of 100 within-category brand-shuffled placebos")

Two conclusions, at different confidence levels. The brand-level relationship is real: the true curve sits above the placebo band across lags, so SoS carries brand-specific information about consideration beyond category-wide seasonality. The lead asymmetry is suggestive but not established: the real +2-vs−2 asymmetry (+0.033) is exceeded by 14 of 100 placebo permutations (p ≈ 0.14). We report it as the pattern you’d expect if search precedes claimed consideration — and note it is directionally consistent with Les Binet’s and Tracksuit’s own published finding that Share of Search leads market share by 6–12 months (see §6). Validating this properly (more waves, holdout prediction) is the single highest-value next step, because a confirmed lead turns SoS into an early-warning metric the survey cannot provide at monthly cost. One caveat applies to any version of this analysis, theirs and ours: media campaigns move awareness, search, and consideration together on different response lags, so lead-lag alone cannot establish causation.

6. Which funnel metric does search actually reflect?

funnel_cmp <- between_cat |>
  select(category_name, Consideration = rho_soc, Awareness = rho_aware,
         `Consideration/Awareness` = rho_conv) |>
  pivot_longer(-category_name, names_to = "metric", values_to = "rho")

ggplot(funnel_cmp, aes(rho, metric, color = metric)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_jitter(height = .12, alpha = .5, size = 1.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = PAL[c(1, 2, 3)], guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Between-brand Spearman ρ vs SoS (one point per category)",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Search resembles awareness as much as consideration",
       subtitle = "Large diamonds = median across categories")

Between brands, SoS correlates with awareness about as strongly as with consideration — funnel shares are heavily collinear across brands (big brands are big everywhere). The sharper test is conversion (consideration ÷ awareness): if SoS only reflected salience, it would not track how well awareness converts to intent. The conversion correlation is positive but weaker — consistent with search sitting between salience and intent.

This is not an inconvenient result — it independently replicates Tracksuit’s own published position. The Tracksuit × Google Return on Awareness study (31 brands, 15 AU/NZ categories, 2024–25) links awareness to Share of Search (~+5pts SoS per +5pts awareness around the 30%-awareness mark, strongest for low/mid awareness brands) and positions SoS as a leading indicator of market share. Our 50-category, 3.5-year study on public data arrives at the same qualitative conclusion from the other direction: SoS behaves as a general brand-demand signal spanning awareness and consideration, not a one-to-one consideration proxy. Practical consequence: present SoS within the awareness → SoS → sales diagnostic stack that study proposes, rather than as a substitute for any single funnel metric. (Their finding of diminishing returns at high awareness also cautions against the linear-share lens for mature brands; a logit-scale sensitivity left for follow-up.)

7. Validation

7.1 Measurement-error robustness: curated vs uncurated terms

naive_vol <- trends_naive |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(mean_idx = mean(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
sos_n <- trends_naive |>
  semi_join(naive_vol |> filter(mean_idx >= VOL_MIN),
            by = c("category_name", "brand_name")) |>
  group_by(category_name, month) |>
  mutate(sos = trends_index / sum(trends_index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()
joined_n <- survey |>
  inner_join(sos_n |> select(category_name, brand_name, month, sos),
             by = c("category_name", "brand_name", "wave_date" = "month")) |>
  group_by(category_name, wave_date) |>
  mutate(soc = consideration / sum(consideration, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()
between_n <- joined_n |>
  group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(sos = mean(sos), soc = mean(soc), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(category_name) |> filter(n() >= 4) |>
  summarise(rho_naive = cor(sos, soc, method = "spearman"), .groups = "drop")

cmp <- between_cat |> select(category_name, rho_curated = rho_soc) |>
  inner_join(between_n, by = "category_name")

ggplot(cmp, aes(rho_naive, rho_curated)) +
  geom_abline(color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = PAL[1], size = 2.4) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Uncurated (raw brand names)", y = "Curated (entities + disambiguation)",
       title = "Curation does not systematically improve category-level correlation",
       subtitle = "Between-brand ρ per category; scatter around the line is large in both directions")

Search-term choice is the largest source of measurement error on the search side, so we re-pull all 507 brands as raw names with no entity resolution and no curation (the --naive flag) and repeat the analysis. This tests whether our conclusions are artifacts of our particular term choices.

The result contradicted our expectation, and that is worth reporting plainly. We expected curation to visibly lift category-level correlations. It does not: median between-brand ρ is 0.53 curated vs 0.55 uncurated, with curation ahead in 23 of 44 categories and a mean gain of +0.003 — a coin flip.

Yet at the brand level the two tiers disagree violently, in both directions:

cv <- trends |> group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(curated = mean(trends_index), .groups = "drop")
nv <- trends_naive |> group_by(category_name, brand_name) |>
  summarise(uncurated = mean(trends_index), .groups = "drop")
cmp_b <- inner_join(cv, nv, by = c("category_name", "brand_name")) |>
  mutate(ratio = (uncurated + .01) / (curated + .01))
bind_rows(
  cmp_b |> slice_max(ratio, n = 5) |>
    mutate(failure = "Uncurated inflated (homonym)"),
  cmp_b |> slice_min(ratio, n = 5) |>
    mutate(failure = "Uncurated missed the brand (punctuation/accent)")
) |>
  select(failure, category_name, brand_name, curated, uncurated) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

Two distinct failure modes, each invisible in the aggregate. Uncurated terms inflate brands whose names are common words — “Ultimate” yoghurt picks up 3,000× its real volume, “Software” skincare 1,900×, “Eva” mattresses, “Grill’d” fast food. They also erase brands whose literal survey spelling is not how people type: “Roll’d” (curly apostrophe), “Kärcher” (umlaut), “Bed Bath N’ Table”, “Temple & Webster” — all read as zero uncurated, all substantial brands in reality.

Why doesn’t this move the category correlations? Because Spearman ρ over 8–15 brands is robust to a few misplaced ones, and the two error types partly offset. The honest conclusion is therefore split by use case:

  • For research conclusions at category level (this study’s claims), the findings are robust to term curation. We would have reached the same verdict with raw terms.
  • For any brand-level product — a client dashboard reading “your Share of Search is 12%” — curation is non-negotiable. An uncurated pipeline would have told a yoghurt brand called Ultimate that it dominated its category, and told Kärcher it did not exist.

That distinction is itself the deliverable: it tells Tracksuit where the data-engineering budget has to go (customer-facing brand metrics) and where it does not (category screening and research).

7.2 Homonym placebo

The failure mode curation prevents, on one brand. Koala is an Australian furniture and mattress company; it is also an animal. The uncurated pull takes the raw term and measures the animal:

hom <- bind_rows(
  trends |> filter(category_name == "Furniture & Homeware", brand_name == "Koala") |>
    mutate(tier = "Curated (topic entity: Koala Sleep Pty Ltd)"),
  trends_naive |> filter(category_name == "Furniture & Homeware", brand_name == "Koala") |>
    mutate(tier = "Uncurated (raw term: \"Koala\")")
)
ggplot(hom, aes(month, raw_index, color = tier)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(PAL[1], PAL[2]), name = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Google Trends index (raw, within batch)",
       title = "The same brand name, two entirely different signals",
       subtitle = "Uncurated 'Koala' tracks tourist and school-holiday interest in the animal")

The two series are barely related. Only the curated one is a measurement of the brand, and the difference is not subtle noise — it is a different subject entirely. Multiply this by the ~100 brands in this sample carrying a common noun, a place name, or a first name, and it is the single largest threat to naive Share-of-Search work.

7.3 Robustness

  • Volume floor sensitivity: the between-brand result is stable across floors — median ρ = 0.44 / 0.46 / 0.47 / 0.46 at floors of 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 5 mean index points (410 / 392 / 342 / 267 brands). Excluding more marginal brands does not manufacture a stronger relationship.
  • Anchor stitching: the pull flags any batch where the anchor brand has no volume (anchor-zero), since the rescaling is then undefined; the final dataset carries zero such flags. Stitch scale factors are logged per batch for audit.
  • Entity-resolution failure is detected, not assumed away: any brand whose topic entity returns an empty series is automatically re-pulled as a raw term (110 brands in the final data), so “no search volume” means no demand rather than a bad identifier. This check was added after QA found ~90 well-known brands (Myer, Big W, TikTok, Liquorland) reading as zero because Google’s autocomplete had offered a dud duplicate entity.
  • Re-pull stability: Trends indices are sampled; repeated pulls of one category on different days shift monthly values by a few index points but leave SoS ranks essentially unchanged.
  • Not tested here (out of timebox, would be next): holdout-wave prediction, other geographies, non-Google search sources, demographic cuts (Trends has none).

8. Recommendation

eligibility <- between_cat |>
  left_join(vol |> group_by(category_name) |>
              summarise(pct_searchable = mean(mean_idx >= VOL_MIN)),
            by = "category_name") |>
  left_join(nd_cat |> select(category_name, survey_reliability = mean_reliability),
            by = "category_name") |>
  mutate(eligible = rho_soc >= .7 & pct_searchable >= .6) |>
  arrange(desc(rho_soc))
eligibility |>
  select(category_name, n_brands, rho_soc, pct_searchable, eligible) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

1. Launch SoS as a complement, in eligible categories. A category qualifies on measurable criteria, not intuition: (a) most of its brands register search volume; (b) SoS reproduces the survey’s brand ranking (ρ ≥ 0.7 in a validation window); (c) brand names are resolvable to clean search entities. Roughly a third of the 50 sampled categories pass today. The product surface: competitive benchmarking between waves, and — pending further validation — a 2–3 month early-warning signal on consideration.

2. Do not substitute. Search has no demographics, no funnel stages, no absolute levels (a relative index cannot say “23% of the category considers you”), and a third of tracked brands are invisible to it. The survey remains the source of truth for levels; search adds frequency and cost-efficiency.

3. Build on the existing Google partnership; treat public Trends as the prototype tier. Tracksuit already works with Google’s aggregated search data (Return on Awareness). Most of the limitations this study documents — relative indices, sampling noise, 5-term batching, invisible long-tail brands, homonym contamination — are artifacts of the free public tier, not of search data itself. The path is therefore: use this study’s methodology (eligibility criteria, noise-aware validation, entity resolution with an auditable log) as the blueprint, and the partnership data as the production source. §7.1 sharpens where that engineering effort belongs: entity resolution is essential for brand-level client reporting and largely irrelevant for category-level screening.

Worked example — a category not in this sample: pet retail (a category I’ve worked in) would likely score well: distinctive brand names (Petbarn, PETstock), a search-heavy purchase journey, and high category interest — the framework predicts eligibility before spending a survey wave to verify.

Appendix: methods detail

  • Stitching: with anchor \(a\) and batch \(k\), each series is scaled by \(\bar{x}_{a,\text{ref}} / \bar{x}_{a,k}\); SoS is then computed within category-month over the searchable brand set.
  • Noise decomposition: for brand \(b\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{noise} = \overline{p_t(1-p_t)/n_t}\); reliability \(= 1 - \hat\sigma^2_{noise} / \hat\sigma^2_{obs}\); the attainable correlation against a noiseless covariate is \(\sqrt{\text{reliability}}\). Weight-based \(n_t\) understates design effects, so ceilings are if anything optimistic.
  • Reproducibility: pull/pull_trends.py --all (and --all --naive) regenerates data/raw/; rmarkdown::render("analysis/report.Rmd") rebuilds this document. Raw pull responses and the resolution log are committed.
  • Limitations: single search source; relative indices; AU only; SoS denominator limited to tracked brands (a competitor outside the tracked set is invisible); intent mix within brand terms (Suncorp banking vs insurance) is unresolved without query-level data.
